Let us recall the integration by part formula:

∫Ω∂f∂xiφ dx+∫Ωf∂φ∂xi dx=∫∂Ωfφ νidΓ\displaystyle \int_{\Omega}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}}\varphi\,dx+\int_{\Omega}f\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial x_{i}}\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}f\varphi\,\nu_{i}d\Gamma∫Ω​∂xi​∂f​φdx+∫Ω​f∂xi​∂φ​dx=∫∂Ω​fφνi​dΓ

where functions are smooth and integrable, and ∂Ω {\partial\Omega}∂Ω is regular. If the RHS vanishes, in particular when the function φ {\varphi}φ is compactly supported in Ω {\Omega}Ω, then

∫Ωf∂φ∂xi dx=−∫Ω∂f∂xiφ dx,\displaystyle \int_{\Omega}f\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial x_{i}}\,dx=-\int_{\Omega}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}}\varphi\,dx,∫Ω​f∂xi​∂φ​dx=−∫Ω​∂xi​∂f​φdx,

and more generally, in multi-index notation

∫Ωf(∂xαφ) dx=(−1)∣α∣∫Ω(∂xαf)φ dx.\displaystyle \int_{\Omega}f(\partial_{x}^{\alpha}\varphi)\,dx=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_{\Omega}(\partial_{x}^{\alpha}f)\varphi\,dx.∫Ω​f(∂xα​φ)dx=(−1)∣α∣∫Ω​(∂xα​f)φdx.

The map (u,v)↦∫Ωuv dx {(u,v)\mapsto\int_{\Omega}uv\,dx}(u,v)↦∫Ω​uvdx is easily seen to be symmetric, bilinear and positive definite, so can be morally viewed as an inner product ⟨u,v⟩ {\langle u,v\rangle}⟨u,v⟩, or more generally, a duality pairing. Then we see from the above that the linear differential operator ∂xα {\partial_{x}^{\alpha}}∂xα​, whose domain is Cc∞(Ω) {C_{c}^{\infty}(\Omega)}Cc∞​(Ω), has its adjoint (−1)∣α∣∂xα {(-1)^{|\alpha|}\partial_{x}^{\alpha}}(−1)∣α∣∂xα​.

While for an ordinary function f {f}f that is merely integrable, the expression ∂xαf {\partial_{x}^{\alpha}f}∂xα​f doesn't make too much sense, however, the expression ∫Ωf(∂xαφ) dx {\int_{\Omega}f(\partial_{x}^{\alpha}\varphi)\,dx}∫Ω​f(∂xα​φ)dx is still well-defined. This suggests an extension of the adjoint operator, initially defined on smooth functions, to a larger space. For that we need to choose a topology on Cc∞(Ω) {C_{c}^{\infty}(\Omega)}Cc∞​(Ω) (one that makes it into a locally convex topological vector space), from which we can get its dual space Cc∞(Ω)′ {C_{c}^{\infty}(\Omega)'}Cc∞​(Ω)′, as the candidate space for extension. The topology should be such that the resulting extension is "reasonable'' enough: if a sequence fn∈Cc∞(Ω) {f_{n}\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\Omega)}fn​∈Cc∞​(Ω) is such that

⟨φ,fn⟩→⟨φ,f⟩\displaystyle \langle\varphi,f_{n}\rangle\rightarrow\langle\varphi,f\rangle⟨φ,fn​⟩→⟨φ,f⟩

holds for all φ∈Cc∞(Ω) {\varphi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\Omega)}φ∈Cc∞​(Ω), which in particular implies

⟨∂xiφ,fn⟩→⟨∂xiφ,f⟩\displaystyle \langle\partial_{x_{i}}\varphi,f_{n}\rangle\rightarrow\langle\partial_{x_{i}}\varphi,f\rangle⟨∂xi​​φ,fn​⟩→⟨∂xi​​φ,f⟩

for all φ∈Cc∞(Ω) {\varphi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\Omega)}φ∈Cc∞​(Ω), then it should hold that

⟨∂xiφ,f⟩=⟨φ,−∂xif⟩\displaystyle \langle\partial_{x_{i}}\varphi,f\rangle=\langle\varphi,-\partial_{x_{i}}f\rangle⟨∂xi​​φ,f⟩=⟨φ,−∂xi​​f⟩

since it holds true for the sequence fn {f_{n}}fn​. In other words, the adjoint operator should be continuously extended, with respect to the duality pairing topology, i.e. the weak* topology. As such, the topology to be placed on Cc∞(Ω) {C_{c}^{\infty}(\Omega)}Cc∞​(Ω) is expected to be very strong, in order for the unbounded operators such as ∂xα {\partial_{x}^{\alpha}}∂xα​ to have a continuous extension. This means that we will get a very large dual space Cc∞(Ω)′ {C_{c}^{\infty}(\Omega)'}Cc∞​(Ω)′, known as the space of distributions on Ω {\Omega}Ω.

This post has been mainly influenced by Terry's notes, where many quotations are from him; also Hörmander's Analysis of linear partial differential operators, Vol. 1, and Stein's several books. The applications of this part of the theory are so fascinating that I decide to devote my next post to them.

1. Generalities

From now we shall focus on the case Ω=Rd {\Omega=\mathbb{R}^{d}}Ω=Rd.

Definition 1 A distribution λ {\lambda}λ in Rd {\mathbb{R}^{d}}Rd is a linear functional on Cc∞(Rd) {C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}Cc∞​(Rd) such that for every compact set K⊂Rd {K\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}}K⊂Rd, there is C=C(K)>0 {C=C(K)>0}C=C(K)>0, k=k(K)∈N {k=k(K)\in\mathbb{N}}k=k(K)∈N such that

∣⟨φ,λ⟩∣≤C∑∣α∣≤ksup⁡∣∂αφ∣(1) \displaystyle |\langle\varphi,\lambda\rangle|\leq C\sum_{|\alpha|\leq k}\sup|\partial^{\alpha}\varphi| (1)∣⟨φ,λ⟩∣≤C∣α∣≤k∑​sup∣∂αφ∣(1)

for all φ∈Cc∞(Rd) {\varphi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}φ∈Cc∞​(Rd).

Being defined by linear duality, a distribution will be studied through testing it against Cc∞(Rd) {C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}Cc∞​(Rd) functions. Thus these functions are often called test functions, when the type of duality is clear.

Note that we always put λ {\lambda}λ into the slot on the right in the duality bracket. The space of distributions is endowed with the conjugate complex structure, that is

⟨φ,cλ⟩=cˉ⟨φ,λ⟩∀c∈C,\displaystyle \langle\varphi,c\lambda\rangle=\bar{c}\langle\varphi,\lambda\rangle\quad\forall c\in\mathbb{C},⟨φ,cλ⟩=cˉ⟨φ,λ⟩∀c∈C,

to keep the analogy with the Hermitian inner product. The continuity condition (1) is equivalent to saying that Cc∞(Rd) {C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}Cc∞​(Rd) is equipped with the smooth topology. The space of distributions Cc∞(Rd)∗ {C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{*}}Cc∞​(Rd)∗, equipped with the corresponding weak* topology, will thus be Hausdorff, thanks to the Hahn-Banach theorem. The weak* convergence for a sequence λn∈Cc∞(Rd)∗ {\lambda_{n}\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{*}}λn​∈Cc∞​(Rd)∗ will be refered to as the convergence in distribution.

Density argument. Suppose the inclusion into some normed vector space

ι:Cc∞(Rd)↪X,\displaystyle \iota:C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\hookrightarrow X,ι:Cc∞​(Rd)↪X,

is continuous and dense. Then the adjoint of this inclusion is a continuous injection into the space of distributions

ι∗:X∗↪Cc∞(Rd)∗,\displaystyle \iota^{*}:X^{*}\hookrightarrow C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{*},ι∗:X∗↪Cc∞​(Rd)∗,

where X∗ {X^{*}}X∗ is equipped with the weak* topology with respect to the topology of X {X}X (objects in X∗ {X^{*}}X∗ can of course be paired up with Cc∞(Rd) {C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}Cc∞​(Rd) functions). Because of the continuous injection, weak* convergence in X∗ {X^{*}}X∗ will imply convergence in the sense of distributions.
We have seen many such situations already, for example:

  • If X=(C0(Rd),∥⋅∥∞) {X=(C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\|\cdot\|_{\infty})}X=(C0​(Rd),∥⋅∥∞​), or X=Cc(Rd) {X=C_{c}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}X=Cc​(Rd), then X∗=M(Rd) {X^{*}=M(\mathbb{R}^{d})}X∗=M(Rd), the space of finite Radon measures, which is the content of the Riesz representation theorem (complex valued case);
  • If X=Lp(Rd) {X=L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}X=Lp(Rd), 1≤p<∞ {1\leq p<\infty}1≤p<∞, then X∗=Lq(Rd) {X^{*}=L^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}X∗=Lq(Rd), with 1/p+1/q=1 {1/p+1/q=1}1/p+1/q=1;
  • If X=S(Rd) {X=\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}X=S(Rd), the space of Schwartz functions, then S(Rd)∗ {\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{*}}S(Rd)∗ is the space of tempered distributions, which will be studied later.

We see that the notion of distribution generalises that of functions and measures. In fact, say a distribution is of order k {k}k if there is a same non-negative integer k {k}k, and not smaller, applies to all compact sets K {K}K in the definition. Then distributions of order 0 can be paired with test functions in the space (C0(Rd),∥⋅∥∞) {(C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\|\cdot\|_{\infty})}(C0​(Rd),∥⋅∥∞​), and thus can be identified with finite Radon measures. Say a distribution λ {\lambda}λ is non-negative if ⟨φ.λ⟩≥0 {\langle\varphi.\lambda\rangle\geq0}⟨φ.λ⟩≥0 for all φ≥0∈Cc∞(Rd) {\varphi\geq0\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}φ≥0∈Cc∞​(Rd), then by density of Cc∞(Rd) {C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}Cc∞​(Rd) in Cc(Rd) {C_{c}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}Cc​(Rd) in the uniform convergence topology, λ {\lambda}λ can again be identified with a non-negative Radon measure, by Riesz representation.
There are distributions that are not Radon measures, nor locally integrable functions. For example:

  • Derivative of the Dirac delta: the distribution

    φ↦−∂xiφ(0)\displaystyle \varphi\mapsto-\partial_{x_{i}}\varphi(0)φ↦−∂xi​​φ(0)

    is of order 1, thus does not arise from a locally integrable function nor a Radon measure.

  • Principal value of 1/x {1/x}1/x: let d=1 {d=1}d=1. The distribution

    φ↦lim⁡ϵ→0∫∣x∣>ϵφ(x)xdx\displaystyle \varphi\mapsto\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow0}\int_{|x|>\epsilon}\frac{\varphi(x)}{x}dxφ↦ϵ→0lim​∫∣x∣>ϵ​xφ(x)​dx

    does not arise from a locally integrable function nor a Radon measure (1/x {1/x}1/x is not locally integrable). Note that the limit exists because of not only the decay of φ {\varphi}φ at infinity, but also that 1/x {1/x}1/x is an odd function that allows to pass the estimate of φ(x)/x {\varphi(x)/x}φ(x)/x near the origin to the difference quotient (φ(x)−φ(0))/x {(\varphi(x)-\varphi(0))/x}(φ(x)−φ(0))/x, which is controled by the derivative of φ {\varphi}φ.

  • Distributional interpretations of 1/∣x∣ {1/|x|}1/∣x∣: let d=1 {d=1}d=1. For any r>0 {r>0}r>0, the distribution

    λr:φ↦∫∣x∣<rφ(x)−φ(0)∣x∣dx+∫∣x∣≥rφ(x)∣x∣dx\displaystyle \lambda_{r}:\varphi\mapsto\int_{|x|<r}\frac{\varphi(x)-\varphi(0)}{|x|}dx+\int_{|x|\geq r}\frac{\varphi(x)}{|x|}dxλr​:φ↦∫∣x∣<r​∣x∣φ(x)−φ(0)​dx+∫∣x∣≥r​∣x∣φ(x)​dx

    does not arise from a locally integrable function nor a Radon measure (1/∣x∣ {1/|x|}1/∣x∣ is not locally integrable). Again, the appearance of φ(x)−φ(0) {\varphi(x)-\varphi(0)}φ(x)−φ(0) makes the first integral convergent. Note that for different r,r′ {r,r'}r,r′, λr {\lambda_{r}}λr​ and λr′ {\lambda_{r'}}λr′​ differ by a constant multiple of the Dirac delta distribution φ↦φ(0) {\varphi\mapsto\varphi(0)}φ↦φ(0).

Let us now set out the rules for manipulating distributions.

Multiplied by a smooth function. We can multiply a test function by a smooth function in the duality bracket (which results in another test function), so we can define the multiplication of a distribution with a smooth function by the adjoint of such an operation:

⟨φ,λh⟩=⟨φ,hλ⟩:=⟨hˉφ,λ⟩\displaystyle \langle\varphi,\lambda h\rangle=\langle\varphi,h\lambda\rangle:=\langle\bar{h}\varphi,\lambda\rangle⟨φ,λh⟩=⟨φ,hλ⟩:=⟨hˉφ,λ⟩

for all test functions φ∈Cc∞(Rd) {\varphi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}φ∈Cc∞​(Rd).

Action of linear bijection. For such a linear transformation L:Rd→Rd {L:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d}}L:Rd→Rd, we can define

⟨φ,λL⟩:=⟨1det⁡Lφ∘L−1,λ⟩.\displaystyle \langle\varphi,\lambda_{L}\rangle:=\langle\frac{1}{\det L}\varphi\circ L^{-1},\lambda\rangle.⟨φ,λL​⟩:=⟨detL1​φ∘L−1,λ⟩.

Convolving with a compactly supported absolutely integrable function. For such a function h {h}h we can define

⟨φ,λ∗h⟩=⟨φ,h∗λ⟩:=⟨φ∗h~,λ⟩\displaystyle \langle\varphi,\lambda*h\rangle=\langle\varphi,h*\lambda\rangle:=\langle\varphi*\tilde{h},\lambda\rangle⟨φ,λ∗h⟩=⟨φ,h∗λ⟩:=⟨φ∗h~,λ⟩

where h~(x):=h(−x)‾ {\tilde{h}(x):=\overline{h(-x)}}h~(x):=h(−x)​. Note that φ∗h~ {\varphi*\tilde{h}}φ∗h~ is again a test function. Moreover, we have the following important result.

Proposition 2 If h∈Cc∞(Rd) {h\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}h∈Cc∞​(Rd), then λ∗h {\lambda*h}λ∗h is a C∞ {C^{\infty}}C∞-function.

Proof: Formally, λ∗h=∫λ(x)h(y−x) dx {\lambda*h=\int\lambda(x)h(y-x)\thinspace dx}λ∗h=∫λ(x)h(y−x)dx is defined and varies smoothly in the y {y}y-variable. It remains to justfy

⟨φ,∫λ(x)h(y−x) dx⟩=⟨∫φh(y−x)‾ dx,λ⟩\displaystyle \langle\varphi,\int\lambda(x)h(y-x)\thinspace dx\rangle=\langle\int\varphi\overline{h(y-x)}\thinspace dx,\lambda\rangle⟨φ,∫λ(x)h(y−x)dx⟩=⟨∫φh(y−x)​dx,λ⟩

for all test functions φ {\varphi}φ. Since λ:Cc∞(Rd)→C {\lambda:C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\rightarrow\mathbb{C}}λ:Cc∞​(Rd)→C is continuous, and the Riemann sum ∑n∈Zdφ(nϵ)h(y−nϵ)‾ {\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}}\varphi(n\epsilon)\overline{h(y-n\epsilon)}}∑n∈Zd​φ(nϵ)h(y−nϵ)​ converges to ∫φh(y−x)‾ {\int\varphi\overline{h(y-x)}}∫φh(y−x)​ in distribution, the desired equality holds by passing to the limit. □ \Box□

We say a sequence of Cc∞ {C_{c}^{\infty}}Cc∞​-functions φn {\varphi_{n}}φn​ forms an approximation to the identity if each φn≥0 {\varphi_{n}\geq0}φn​≥0, ∫φn dx=1 {\int\varphi_{n}\thinspace dx=1}∫φn​dx=1, and the support shrinks to the origin. Since

∫ψ(x)φn(x) dx=ψ(0)∫B(0,r)φn(x) dx+o(r)→ψ(0)\displaystyle \int\psi(x)\varphi_{n}(x)\thinspace dx=\psi(0)\int_{B(0,r)}\varphi_{n}(x)\thinspace dx+o(r)\rightarrow\psi(0)∫ψ(x)φn​(x)dx=ψ(0)∫B(0,r)​φn​(x)dx+o(r)→ψ(0)

we see that the sequence φn {\varphi_{n}}φn​ converges to the Dirac delta φn→δ {\varphi_{n}\rightarrow\delta}φn​→δ in distribution. What is more, we have the following useful facts

Lemma 3 Let φn {\varphi_{n}}φn​ be an approximation to the identity.

*- If f∈Cc∞(Rd) {f\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}f∈Cc∞​(Rd), then f∗φn→f {f*\varphi_{n}\rightarrow f}f∗φn​→f in the smooth topology;

  • If f∈C(Rd) {f\in C(\mathbb{R}^{d})}f∈C(Rd), then f∗φn→f {f*\varphi_{n}\rightarrow f}f∗φn​→f uniformly on compact sets;
  • If f∈Lp(Rd) {f\in L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}f∈Lp(Rd), 1≤p<∞ {1\leq p<\infty}1≤p<∞, then f∗φn→f {f*\varphi_{n}\rightarrow f}f∗φn​→f in Lp {L^{p}}Lp.*

As a corollary of (1), we see that the test function space Cc∞(Rd) {C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}Cc∞​(Rd) is dense in the space of distributions. Thus operations on test functions that is continuous with respect to the distributional topology can be extended to distributions.

Differentiation of distributions. As motivated in the begining, the differentiation of a distribution λ {\lambda}λ can be defined by

⟨φ,Pλ⟩=⟨P∗φ,λ⟩\displaystyle \langle\varphi,P\lambda\rangle=\langle P^{*}\varphi,\lambda\rangle⟨φ,Pλ⟩=⟨P∗φ,λ⟩

where P {P}P is any linear partial differential operator with smooth coefficients, and P∗ {P^{*}}P∗ is the adjoint operator of P {P}P. If P {P}P is a partial derivative operator, the distribution Pλ {P\lambda}Pλ obtained is called a distributional derivative. If a distributional derivative happens to be a locally integrable function, then it is called a weak derivative. Since these operators are continuous in the distributional topology, a number of manipulations with derivatives, e.g. the product rule, continue to hold whenever the product is allowed in the distributional topology.

Many non-smooth functions have distributional derivatives that make sense intuitively. For example, the locally integrable function H(x)=χ(0,∞) {H(x)=\chi_{(0,\infty)}}H(x)=χ(0,∞)​ is called the Heaviside function. Its distributional derivative is the Dirac delta measure δ0 {\delta_{0}}δ0​ at the origin, since by the fundamental theorem of calculus

∫Rφ(x)H′(x) dx=−∫Rφ′(x)H(x) dx=φ(0).\displaystyle \int_{\mathbb{R}}\varphi(x)H'(x)\,dx=-\int_{\mathbb{R}}\varphi'(x)H(x)\,dx=\varphi(0).∫R​φ(x)H′(x)dx=−∫R​φ′(x)H(x)dx=φ(0).

It's also easy to see that the distributional derivative of χ(a,b) {\chi_{(a,b)}}χ(a,b)​ is the signed measure δa−δb {\delta_{a}-\delta_{b}}δa​−δb​, since

∫Rφ(x)χ(a,b)′(x) dx=−∫φ′(x)χ(a,b)(x) dx=φ(a)−φ(b).\displaystyle \int_{\mathbb{R}}\varphi(x)\chi_{(a,b)}'(x)\,dx=-\int\varphi'(x)\chi_{(a,b)}(x)\,dx=\varphi(a)-\varphi(b).∫R​φ(x)χ(a,b)′​(x)dx=−∫φ′(x)χ(a,b)​(x)dx=φ(a)−φ(b).

We also have the high dimensional analog of the above, known as the Gauss-Green formula, or divergence theorem. Assume that Ω⊂Rd {\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}}Ω⊂Rd is an open set with C1 {C^{1}}C1-boundary, then it holds that

∫Rd(∂jφ)χΩ dx=−∫∂ΩφνjdΓ,(2) \displaystyle \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}(\partial_{j}\varphi)\chi_{\Omega}\,dx=-\int_{\partial\Omega}\varphi\nu_{j}d\Gamma, (2)∫Rd​(∂j​φ)χΩ​dx=−∫∂Ω​φνj​dΓ,(2)

where νj {\nu_{j}}νj​ is the j {j}j-th component of the unit outward normal vector, and dΓ {d\Gamma}dΓ is the Euclidean surface measure on ∂Ω {\partial\Omega}∂Ω. Thus we have the distributional equality

∂jχS=νjdΓ.\displaystyle \partial_{j}\chi_{S}=\nu_{j}d\Gamma.∂j​χS​=νj​dΓ.

The Fourier transform on tempered distributions. The Schwartz space S(Rd) {\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}S(Rd) consists of smooth functions with all their derivatives rapidly decreasing at infinity. The topology is given by the family of norms indexed in N≥0 {N\geq0}N≥0,

∥φ∥N=sup⁡x∈Rd,∣α∣,∣β∣≤N∣xβ(∂xαφ)(x)∣.\displaystyle \|\varphi\|_{N}=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d},|\alpha|,|\beta|\leq N}|x^{\beta}(\partial_{x}^{\alpha}\varphi)(x)|.∥φ∥N​=x∈Rd,∣α∣,∣β∣≤Nsup​∣xβ(∂xα​φ)(x)∣.

A tempered distribution is a continuous linear functional on S(Rd) {\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}S(Rd). Since the Fourier transform

F:φ↦φ∧(ξ)=∫Rdφ(x)e−2πix⋅ξ dx\displaystyle \mathcal{F}:\varphi\mapsto\varphi^{\wedge}(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\varphi(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\thinspace dxF:φ↦φ∧(ξ)=∫Rd​φ(x)e−2πix⋅ξdx

is a continuous bijection on S(Rd) {\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}S(Rd), whose inverse is given by

F:ψ↦ψ∨(x)=∫Rdψ(ξ)e2πix⋅ξ dξ,\displaystyle \mathcal{F}:\psi\mapsto\psi^{\vee}(x)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\psi(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\thinspace d\xi,F:ψ↦ψ∨(x)=∫Rd​ψ(ξ)e2πix⋅ξdξ,

we define

⟨φ,λ∧⟩=⟨φ∨,λ⟩\displaystyle \langle\varphi,\lambda^{\wedge}\rangle=\langle\varphi^{\vee},\lambda\rangle⟨φ,λ∧⟩=⟨φ∨,λ⟩

as the inverse of the Fourier transform is also its adjoint, under the complex conjugate structure on the space of tempered distributions. The Fourier transform will be studied in greater details in a separate section. Before that we just note several facts regarding the tempered distributions.

A C∞ {C^{\infty}}C∞-function ψ {\psi}ψ is said to be increasing slowly if for each multi-index α {\alpha}α, ∣∂αψ∣=O(∣x∣Nα) {|\partial^{\alpha}\psi|=O(|x|^{N_{\alpha}})}∣∂αψ∣=O(∣x∣Nα​) for some Nα≥0 {N_{\alpha}\geq0}Nα​≥0. The product of a tempered distribution with a slowly increasing C∞ {C^{\infty}}C∞-function is still tempered. A tempered distribution convolving with a Schwartz function is a slowly increasing C∞ {C^{\infty}}C∞-function. A distribution λ {\lambda}λ is said to be supported on a closed set F {F}F if its complement Fc {F^{c}}Fc is the largest open set such that

⟨φ,λ⟩=0\displaystyle \langle\varphi,\lambda\rangle=0⟨φ,λ⟩=0

whenever φ {\varphi}φ is supported within Fc {F^{c}}Fc. A distribution with compact support is easily seen to be tempered. In particular this is the case for the Dirac delta distribution, whose support is the singleton {0} {\{0\}}{0}. Such distribution is said to have point support. A compactly supported distribution convolving with a Schwartz function remains a Schwartz function. From this, we can even define convolutions of tempered distributions with compactly supported distributions.

A final remark: in general, one cannot perform non-linear operations on distributions, such as taking absolute value, and multiplication of distribution with anything rougher than a smooth function. In the former case, there is no good sense of adjointness to those operations, and in the latter, in whose possible definition does not always lead to a proper test function.

2. The Fourier transform in Rd {\mathbb{R}^{d}}Rd; the action of translation

We start by noting the intimate relation between the Fourier transform in the Euclidean space Rd {\mathbb{R}^{d}}Rd and a naturual group action on it, namely, the translation by an element of Rd {\mathbb{R}^{d}}Rd

τx:y↦y−x.\displaystyle \tau_{x}:y\mapsto y-x.τx​:y↦y−x.

The action naturally introduces a linear operator on functions defined on the Euclidean space, by

τxf(y):=f(y−x).\displaystyle \tau_{x}f(y):=f(y-x).τx​f(y):=f(y−x).
